notes.definition: Waste water from homes, farms and industry must be treated before it is released into the environment. Sewage treatment removes solids, organic matter and harmful microbes using screening, sedimentation, anaerobic digestion of sludge and aerobic biological treatment of effluent.
explanation: Urban lifestyles and industrial processes produce large amounts of waste water. This water must be treated before being released back into the environment, for example into rivers or the sea. Sewage and agricultural waste water contain organic matter (such as human waste, food and animal waste) and harmful microbes, which must be removed. Industrial waste water may also contain organic matter and harmful chemicals (such as toxic metal compounds) that need to be removed.

Sewage treatment begins with screening and grit removal. The sewage passes through a mesh screen that removes large objects such as rags, plastics and paper, and grit (sand and small stones) is allowed to settle out. These materials would block pipes or damage machinery later in the process.

Next comes sedimentation. The sewage is left to stand in large settlement tanks. Heavier solids sink to the bottom to form sewage sludge, while the lighter liquid on top, called effluent, is removed from the top of the tank. The sludge and the effluent are then treated separately.

The sewage sludge is treated by anaerobic digestion. In digesters, bacteria break down the organic matter in the absence of oxygen. This produces biogas (mainly methane), which can be burned as a fuel to generate electricity for the treatment works, and a digested solid that can be used as a fertiliser on farmland. The effluent undergoes aerobic biological treatment: air is bubbled through it so that aerobic bacteria break down the remaining organic matter and harmful microbes. The treated water is then clean enough to be released into rivers or the sea.

You need to be able to compare the ease of obtaining potable water from waste water, ground water and salt water. Ground water (from aquifers) is usually the easiest: it is fresh water that has been naturally filtered through rock, so it mainly needs filtering and sterilising. Waste water needs many more stages to remove organic matter and microbes, so it uses more energy, and many people find drinking recycled sewage unacceptable. Salt water has to be desalinated by distillation or reverse osmosis, which requires large amounts of energy. Where fresh water is scarce, treating waste water or desalinating sea water may be necessary.
keyFacts: Urban lifestyles and industry produce large amounts of waste water that must be treated before release.
Sewage and agricultural waste water need organic matter and harmful microbes removed.
Industrial waste water may also need harmful chemicals removed.
Stage 1: screening and grit removal (removes large objects and grit).
Stage 2: sedimentation separates sewage sludge (bottom) from effluent (liquid on top).
Sludge is treated by anaerobic digestion (bacteria, no oxygen), producing biogas (methane) and fertiliser.
Effluent is treated by aerobic biological treatment (air bubbled through, bacteria break down organic matter).
Ground water is usually the easiest source of potable water; waste water and salt water need more processing and energy.

keyTerms.definition: Water that has been used in homes, agriculture or industry and contains contaminants.
Waste water from homes and businesses, containing human waste, organic matter and microbes.
Passing sewage through a mesh to remove large objects such as rags, plastics and paper.
Leaving sewage to stand so that heavier solids sink to form sludge, leaving liquid effluent above.
The solid material that settles at the bottom of sedimentation tanks.
The liquid that is removed from the top of sedimentation tanks.
Breakdown of organic matter by bacteria in the absence of oxygen, producing biogas (methane).
Bubbling air through effluent so that aerobic bacteria break down organic matter and harmful microbes.

workedExamples.title: Ordering the stages of sewage treatment
workedExamples.question: Put these stages in order and say what each removes or produces: aerobic biological treatment of effluent, screening, sedimentation, anaerobic digestion of sludge.
steps: Screening comes first, removing large objects and grit.
Sedimentation separates the remaining sewage into sludge and effluent.

The two parts are treated separately: sludge by anaerobic digestion (producing biogas and fertiliser) and effluent by aerobic biological treatment (breaking down remaining organic matter and microbes).
workedExamples.answer: Screening and grit removal → sedimentation → anaerobic digestion of sludge and aerobic treatment of effluent (these last two happen in parallel).

workedExamples.title: Interpreting treatment data
workedExamples.question: Waste water entering a works contains 400 mg/dm³ of organic matter. After treatment it contains 20 mg/dm³. Calculate the percentage of organic matter removed.

workedExamples.title: Choosing a source of potable water
workedExamples.question: A coastal town in a dry region can use ground water (limited supply), treated waste water or sea water. Compare the ease of obtaining potable water from each.
steps: Ground water: naturally filtered, needs only filtering and sterilising, so easiest and cheapest, but supply is limited.
Waste water: needs screening, sedimentation, biological treatment and then further purification and sterilising; uses more energy and may not be acceptable to the public.
Sea water: plentiful, but desalination by distillation or reverse osmosis needs large amounts of energy.
workedExamples.answer: Ground water is easiest; waste water and sea water need much more processing and energy, but may be needed when ground water runs short.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think sedimentation removes microbes from sewage.
misconceptions.right: In fact sedimentation only separates solids (sludge) from liquid (effluent); microbes and dissolved organic matter are broken down later by bacteria in biological treatment.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often mix up which part is treated aerobically.
misconceptions.right: In fact the effluent has air bubbled through it (aerobic); the sludge is digested without oxygen (anaerobic).

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think bacteria are only harmful in sewage treatment.
misconceptions.right: In fact useful bacteria carry out both anaerobic digestion and aerobic biological treatment, breaking down organic matter and harmful microbes.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think treated sewage effluent is potable.
misconceptions.right: In fact treated effluent is clean enough to release into rivers, but it would need further purification and sterilising to be safe to drink.

realWorld: Many UK sewage works burn the methane biogas from anaerobic digesters to generate electricity for the works.
Digested sewage sludge is spread on farmland as a fertiliser and soil improver.
Singapore treats waste water with membranes and UV to produce 'NEWater', reducing reliance on imported water.
examTips: Learn the four stages in order: screening and grit removal, sedimentation, anaerobic digestion of sludge, aerobic biological treatment of effluent.
Use the words 'sludge' and 'effluent' precisely: sludge is the settled solid, effluent is the liquid.
Link 'anaerobic' with sludge and 'aerobic' with effluent; a common mark is lost by swapping them.
When comparing sources of potable water, mention energy and the number of treatment stages; ground water is usually easiest.
summary: Waste water must be treated before release into the environment.
Sewage and agricultural waste: remove organic matter and harmful microbes.
Industrial waste: may also need harmful chemicals removed.
Screening and grit removal, then sedimentation into sludge and effluent.
Sludge: anaerobic digestion. Effluent: aerobic biological treatment.
Ground water is easiest to make potable; waste water and sea water need more processing.

markScheme: 1 mark: Aerobic biological treatment
questions.explanation: Air is bubbled through the effluent so aerobic bacteria break down organic matter. Anaerobic digestion is for the sludge.

questions.question: What does 'anaerobic' mean in anaerobic digestion?
markScheme: 1 mark: without oxygen
questions.explanation: Anaerobic bacteria break down sludge in sealed digesters with no oxygen, producing methane.

questions.question: Which type of waste water is most likely to contain harmful chemicals such as toxic metal compounds?
markScheme: 1 mark: industrial waste water
questions.explanation: Industrial processes can release harmful chemicals, which must be removed as well as organic matter.

questions.question: Which source usually needs the fewest treatment stages to produce potable water?
markScheme: 1 mark: Ground water
questions.explanation: Ground water is fresh water naturally filtered through rock, so it mainly needs filtering and sterilising.

questions.question: Why is air bubbled through the effluent during aerobic biological treatment?
options: To push solid sludge to the bottom of the tank
To provide oxygen for bacteria that break down organic matter
To remove dissolved salts as a gas
To sterilise the water with nitrogen
markScheme: 1 mark: provides oxygen for (aerobic) bacteria to break down organic matter
questions.explanation: Aerobic bacteria need oxygen to respire as they break down organic matter and harmful microbes.

questions.question: A water company says anaerobic digestion makes sewage treatment more sustainable. Which reason supports this?
options: It removes all the microbes from the effluent
It produces methane that can be used as a fuel, and a solid that can be used as fertiliser
It turns sludge into potable water
markScheme: 1 mark: methane fuel and fertiliser are produced
questions.explanation: Useful products are recovered from waste, reducing the need for other fuels and fertilisers.

questions.question: Why are rags and plastics removed by screening at the start of sewage treatment?
options: They would block pipes and damage machinery
They are needed for anaerobic digestion
They contain microbes that clean the water
markScheme: 1 mark: they would block pipes / damage equipment
questions.explanation: Large objects are not broken down by bacteria and would cause blockages.

questions.explanation: Anaerobic bacteria digest the organic matter in sealed tanks.

questions.question: Explain why industrial waste water may need extra treatment compared with sewage from homes.
markScheme: 1 mark: industrial waste water may contain harmful chemicals (for example toxic metal compounds)
1 mark: these are not removed by biological treatment and must be removed before release
questions.explanation: Bacteria break down organic matter, but toxic chemicals need other methods to remove them.

questions.question: Explain why waste water must be treated before it is released into rivers.
markScheme: 1 mark: it contains harmful microbes that could spread disease
1 mark: organic matter / harmful chemicals would pollute the river and harm living organisms
questions.explanation: Untreated sewage spreads disease and organic matter is broken down by microbes that use up oxygen in the river, harming fish.

questions.question: Suggest why treating waste water to make potable water is less common than treating ground water, even though waste water is available in large amounts.
markScheme: 1 mark: waste water needs many more treatment stages (to remove organic matter, microbes and chemicals)
1 mark: so it uses more energy and costs more
1 mark: many people are unwilling to drink water made from sewage
questions.explanation: Ground water is already fairly clean, so it is cheaper and more acceptable to use.

questions.question: A student says sedimentation makes the effluent safe to drink. Explain why the student is wrong.
markScheme: 1 mark: effluent still contains dissolved organic matter and harmful microbes
1 mark: it needs aerobic biological treatment (and further purification and sterilising) before it could be safe
questions.explanation: Sedimentation only lets heavy solids settle; it does not remove dissolved or tiny suspended material or kill microbes.

questions.question:
Describe how sewage is treated so that the water can be safely released into a river.
Include the names of the stages and what happens at each stage.
markScheme: Indicative content: screening removes large objects such as rags and plastics; grit removal lets sand and stones settle; sedimentation in settlement tanks; heavy solids sink as sewage sludge; liquid effluent removed from the top; sludge undergoes anaerobic digestion by bacteria without oxygen; biogas (methane) produced and used as fuel; digested sludge used as fertiliser; effluent undergoes aerobic biological treatment; air bubbled through so bacteria break down organic matter and harmful microbes; treated water released.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): all stages in the correct order with clear description of what happens to both sludge and effluent, using aerobic and anaerobic correctly.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): most stages described, with some detail, but possibly with minor errors in order or terms.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): one or two stages named or simple descriptions.
questions.explanation: The key is the split after sedimentation: sludge goes to anaerobic digestion, effluent to aerobic treatment.

questions.question:
A town in a dry, coastal region needs more drinking water. It could use ground water, treated waste water or desalinated sea water.
Compare the ease of obtaining potable water from these three sources.
markScheme: Indicative content: ground water is naturally filtered so only needs filtering and sterilising, lowest energy and cost, but supply may be limited in a dry region; waste water needs screening, sedimentation, biological treatment, then further purification and sterilising, more energy and possible public objections; sea water is plentiful on the coast but desalination by distillation or reverse osmosis needs large amounts of energy and is expensive.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): clear comparison of all three sources, referring to the processing needed and energy or cost.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements about one or two sources.
questions.explanation: Comparisons should rank the sources and give reasons linked to treatment steps and energy.

questions.question:

markScheme: 1 mark: Effluent
questions.explanation: Effluent is the liquid; sludge is the settled solid.

questions.question: State what is used to break down organic matter in both the sludge and the effluent.
markScheme: 1 mark: bacteria (microorganisms)
questions.explanation: Useful bacteria break down organic matter: anaerobic bacteria in sludge, aerobic bacteria in effluent.

questions.question: Suggest why the solid left after anaerobic digestion is useful as a fertiliser on farmland.
markScheme: 1 mark: it contains nutrients (for example nitrogen and phosphorus compounds)
1 mark: which plants need for growth / so less manufactured fertiliser is needed
questions.explanation: Human waste is rich in nitrogen and phosphorus compounds, which remain in the digested sludge.
